vignette:
Marcus Heller had spent twenty-three years building the kind of school where children felt safe. As principal of a mid-sized public elementary school in suburban Ohio, he was known for his open-door policy, his steady presence in the hallways, and his habit of greeting every student by name. That reputation, and the life it represented, began to fracture on a Tuesday afternoon in late October when a parent he had been in ongoing conflict with over a disciplinary matter forced his way past the front office and cornered Marcus alone in his office. What followed lasted less than four minutes. The man was larger than Marcus, and he came with his hands already moving. Marcus was struck repeatedly, thrown against the corner of his own desk, and pinned against the wall with a forearm pressed across his throat before a custodian heard the commotion and intervened. The police came. A report was filed. The man was removed. And Marcus drove himself home that evening because he told himself he was fine.

He was not fine. In the weeks that followed, something had reorganized itself inside him in ways he could not name or fully locate. Sleep became shallow and then almost impossible. He would lie still beside his wife, Diane, and find himself cataloguing the sounds of the house - the furnace cycling on, a car slowing outside - each one arriving with a jolt of electricity through his chest that left him rigid and breathless. The startle responses came without warning during the day too: a student dropping a textbook in the hallway, a door swinging open behind him. Each time, his body responded as though the thing that happened in October was happening again right now.

When memories surfaced - and they surfaced constantly, uninvited, running in a loop with the quality of footage he could not switch off - Marcus noticed something that disturbed him almost as much as the memories themselves. He could feel his body returning to the position it had been in when the man had him against the wall. The pressure across his throat seemed to reconstitute itself. His shoulders would draw in, his chin would tuck, and he would find himself braced against something that was no longer there. Yet when he tried to sit down and deliberately think through what had happened - to get some kind of handle on it, to reconstruct the sequence - the memory became strangely inaccessible, slipping away from him like something underwater. He had come to believe that this gap meant something was wrong with him at a deeper level, that his mind was concealing something he was not equipped to face.

At school, the changes were impossible to ignore, though Marcus worked hard to ensure no one else noticed them. He had come to believe that any room he entered could become what his office had become, and so he made a habit - compulsive and immediate - of locating the exits the moment he walked through a door. Staff meetings, the gymnasium, the cafeteria: he positioned himself accordingly. He also found himself registering objects he had never thought about before. A letter opener on a secretary's desk. A fire extinguisher bracket in the hallway. A pair of scissors left out during an art class. He was certain that noticing these things was necessary, that the failure to notice them was what had made him vulnerable in October. What frightened him most was not the objects themselves but the implication of their presence - that danger was already distributed throughout the building he was supposed to protect.

By spring, Diane had begun asking questions he could not answer. He had stopped attending the neighbourhood gatherings they had always enjoyed together. He had cancelled a weekend trip twice. She told him, gently and then with more urgency, that he had become someone who stood with his back to walls.

It was Diane, ultimately, who found the name of a therapist and sat with him while he made the appointment. Marcus came to the first session carrying the particular exhaustion of a man who had spent seven months managing something he could not see clearly. What he most hoped for was to stop scanning every room he walked into. What he most feared was that someone would confirm what he had quietly suspected since October - that the man who had run that school with such steadiness no longer existed.
